description: We are a team of polish students from TU Delft, mixed between aerospace and computer science.
summary: The Earth Jukebox is a webtool built to support the communities for who typical means of visualization are limited in effectiveness. It does this through sonification : the use of non-speech audio to convey information or represent data. The website proposes an array of models based on visualizations from NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio prepared for the Earth Information Center (EIC).  These sounds were synthesized through a combination of custom sound samples built by our team. The user can also choose to create his own soundtrack through the web-tool, needing only a visualization video and corresponding bar-chart needed to read it. The aim is to empower anyone to create their own videos, a pillar of the human right of information.  Full project details are available on the teams GitHub : https://github.com/krecony/nasa
details:
Earth Jukebox turns NASA Earth visualizations into music, so that changes in rain, wind and temperature can be heard as well as seen. We built it for the NASA Space Apps 2026 Earth Information Jukebox Challenge. Visitors can listen to the published tracks on our website and create their own sonifications from other NASA videos.

The website opens on an interactive 3D forest drawn in WebGL that reacts to the movement of the cursor. Pressing “Check it out” flies the camera over the treetops to a hidden clearing, where the jukebox lies on the forest floor. There, visitors choose between three published tracks, each built from a NASA visualization of the whole Earth. In the Global Rain and Snow track, made from NASA’s IMERG precipitation data, rain is heard as plucked notes, heavy downpours as thunder, and snow as bells. In the Near-Surface Wind Speed track, from the GEOS-FP weather model, wind speed becomes whistles and storms become wind chimes. In the Near-Surface Temperature track, also from GEOS-FP, temperature is carried by held voices, very hot regions by plucks, and freezing areas by the sound of wind. Each track plays as a video with its soundtrack, and captions that describe what is happening each day can be switched on in the video controls.

Behind the tracks is a Python pipeline that reads the visualization frame by frame. It uses the visualization’s own color legend to turn each pixel’s color back into the value it represents, such as millimeters of rain per hour or degrees of temperature. These values are then turned into music through pitch, volume, rhythm and stereo position, so that where and how strongly something happens on the map shapes what the listener hears. For every track the pipeline produces the soundtrack, plots and a CSV file of the extracted data, the daily captions, and a video combining the original visualization with the music.

Anyone can also create their own track. The public studio runs the same Python engine directly in the visitor’s browser through Pyodide, so no software needs to be installed and no video is ever uploaded: all processing happens on the visitor’s own computer. A user adds a NASA video, defines its color scale, chooses the sounds, previews the result and publishes it to their jukebox. Custom tracks are kept in that browser’s storage, appear alongside the published tracks, and can be exported and imported as ZIP files to share with others.

The project can also be run locally. Serving the website folder with Python’s built-in web server is enough to use the jukebox and the in-browser studio. With Python 3.11 or newer and FFmpeg installed, the local studio (studio.py) adds a version that saves tracks to disk and publishes them to the local website. Tracks can also be built from the command line with sonify.py. Each track lives in its own folder with two settings files: one describing the video, its color scale and timing, and one describing the instruments and how data maps to sound. Custom WAV recordings can be used as instruments, and the video analysis is cached so sounds can be adjusted quickly.

The code is organized into the static website (the WebGL forest, the player and the browser studio), a shared jukebox package containing the analysis, synthesis, caption and studio logic, the local studio server, the track generator, and the track settings and instrument samples. The website is deployed automatically to GitHub Pages.

The visualizations come from the NASA Scientific Visualization Studio and the Earth Information Center.
